commentary
What will Trump do after the midterms, with nothing left to lose?
Expect lies, threats and empty bluster. He's becoming politically insignificant — but still dangerous
By
Brian Karem
White House columnist
Published
October 9, 2026 9:05AM (EDT)
Donald Trump dances as he leaves the stage after speaking at the Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio, Oct. 7, 2026. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
On Wednesday in the Oval Office, Donald Trump made clear that he’s not happy with how his political rivals have treated him and stoutly reserved his right for revenge. “They impeached me twice. I certainly — even to this moment I can do whatever I want, if I want.” Trump said, before claiming that only his respect for the office of the president keeps his behavior in check.
If this were a sitcom— and it feels like a bad one — we would now hear a laugh track followed by groans.
Clearly Trump has never understood the foundational concepts of American politics. Political ethics, the art of “half a loaf,” the truism that “all politics are local” and the principles of public service over private enrichment are lost on him. Those are just sayings on trophies Trump has minted for himself since he’ll never get the Nobel Peace Prize.
He certainly doesn’t understand compromise or the importance of local issues. Consider his enthusiastic support for data centers, the only issue currently uniting Americans. He’s too busy feathering his own nest while laughing off any pretense of ethical behavior. While we can certainly criticize Trump for ignoring the foundations of our democracy, the same could also be said of Congress, most state houses and many city councils. And, hey, let’s not talk about the local pool board. That’s where stuff really gets weird. Sometime I’ll tell you about my former neighbor in Gaithersburg who thought “Robert’s Rules of Order” had something to do with sharing spouses.
Recent polls of likely voters in the midterm elections make it clear that a significant majority are extremely tired of the nonsense promulgated by Trump and others. Yeah, those are just polls and they only offer you a vague snapshot in time. That being said, it isn’t just about the polls. Donald Trump is so scared of what’s coming that he’s limited his campaign activities to shoring up support in the deepest red districts of America while threatening Democrats with hellfire and damnation.
No one could be more delighted than the Democratic National Committee, whose pitch to the electorate consists of three words: “We’re not him!” It’s a simple message, if not exactly an inspiring one, made possible by Trump’s overwhelmingly inept corruption. At least for now, the Republicans have lowered the bar so far under a despotic president that even the dysfunctional Democrats might crawl over it.

Trump Turns 80: Six Accomplishments and Six Controversies That Still Define His Legacy
From Supreme Court appointments to impeachment and criminal conviction, his record remains deeply divisive.
By Jeanna Francis
June 15, 2026 14:48 +08
Donald J. Trump Turns 80
X/ Mario Nawfal @MarioNawfal
On June 14, 2026, Donald John Trump turned 80. He is, by any measure, the most singular figure in modern American political history: the only person to serve as both the 45th and 47th President of the United States, the first to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives, the first former president to be convicted of a felony, and the man who has dominated American political sphere more vibrantly than any figure since Franklin D. Roosevelt.
Polling from the Pew Research Center consistently shows the country split nearly down the middle on his legacy and has for a decade. On the day he turns 80, that division is no narrower than the day he first descended the golden escalator at Trump Tower 11 years ago.
A balanced account of his career requires holding two things in mind: he has achieved things that endured, and he has done things that his harshest critics argue came closer to ending American democracy. Here is a factual check in six of each:
SIX ACCOMPLISHMENTS
1. Reshaped the Supreme Court
Trump appointed three Supreme Court justices in a single term: Neil Gorsuch in 2017, Brett Kavanaugh in 2018, and Amy Coney Barrett in 2020, creating a 6-3 conservative majority that has since reshaped American constitutional law on abortion, gun rights, administrative regulation and executive power.
The appointments, confirmed by the US Senate and recorded in full on the US Courts website, represent perhaps the most durable consequence of his first term. No president since Franklin Roosevelt had altered the court's ideological composition so dramatically in a single four-year period.
"President Trump fundamentally changed the direction of the federal judiciary," noted a 2022 Congressional Research Service analysis of his appointments.
2. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (2017)
Signed into law on December 22, 2017, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, verified on Congress website, was the most sweeping overhaul of the US tax code since 1986. It cut the corporate tax rate from 35% to 21%, doubled the standard deduction, and restructured individual tax brackets.
Supporters credit it with fueling a period of low unemployment and strong corporate investment before the pandemic. Critics, including the Congressional Budget Office, noted it added an estimated $1.9 trillion to the national debt over ten years.
3. The Abraham Accords
In September 2020, the Trump administration brokered normalization agreements between Israel and the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, the first Arab-Israeli normalization deals in 26 years, following the Egypt and Jordan agreements of 1979 and 1994.
